Q49289829.summary: On this broken fragment a boat full of small figures rides the waves above, while below two figures stand on the water: Christ reaching toward Peter, who has stepped out to meet him. Painted for the baptistery of the house church at Dura-Europos, the scene told new believers that just as Christ held Peter above the waves of Galilee, he would save those who passed through the waters of baptism.
facts: Because two figures appear on the water, the scene follows Matthew's account, in which Peter also walks on the sea, rather than the versions in Mark and John where Jesus walks alone.
The fragment (about 139 × 100 cm) is one of three Dura-Europos paintings counted among the earliest surviving images of Jesus, together with the Good Shepherd and the Healing of the Paralytic.
The scene was only partly preserved because the wall above it had been torn down when the city's defences were reinforced.

cur:catacombs2-narbonne-good-shepherd-sa.summary: Between two broad fields of wavy strigils, a small central panel shows the Good Shepherd standing between two trees, his sheep at his feet. Worn and flattened, the relief still conveys the gentle simplicity of the image that, more than any other, expressed the Early Christian hope of being carried home by Christ.
facts: The museum label recorded on Commons attributes it to a Narbonne workshop and records its discovery on the Avenue de l'Hérault in Narbonne.

wga:zearly/1/5coptic/painting/1bawit2.summary: Painted in the niche of a chapel in one of Egypt's great desert monasteries, the upper zone shows Christ enthroned in a glowing mandorla, holding a book and blessing, flanked by medallions of the sun and moon and by heavenly beings; below, the Virgin Mary stands among the apostles and other saints. The two-tiered composition joins heaven and earth, the ascended Lord above and the Church gathered in prayer below. With its large eyes, frontal poses and bold, simple colours, it is a masterpiece of Coptic painting and a vivid witness to the faith of Egyptian monks.
facts: The monastery of Apa Apollo at Bawit was excavated by French archaeologists, led by Jean Clédat, in the early 1900s; its finds were divided between the Coptic Museum in Cairo and the Louvre.
The two-zone scheme of Christ in glory above the Virgin and apostles was widely used in Coptic monastic chapels and is often read as a combined image of the Ascension and the Second Coming.
Greek labels identify the busts beside Christ as Helios and Selene, the sun and moon, witnesses to their Creator's glory, as in many early images of the Ascension and Crucifixion.
Bawit also produced the famous icon of Christ and Abbot Mena, now in the Louvre, featured earlier in this journey.
wga:zearly/1/5coptic/painting/1bawit2.notes: The exact chapel number at Bawit was not verified. Date broadened to 6th–7th century, the monastery's period of prosperity; WGA gives '6th century'. The identification of the creatures at the edges is general, as they are only partly visible.
